title: Same Meaning, Different Word
blurb: Understand reference words in a text

steps.html:
Three of the four things people say about the moon are nonsense. The fourth sounds the most like a story and happens to be true. Along the way: the small words — this, that, it, one, such, do so — that hold a text together, and that most readers skip.

  • Work out what a reference word refers back to
  • Use synonyms and antonyms precisely
  • Read for the writer's real position, not the surface claim
  • Write a text that holds together without repeating itself

steps.title: The small words that hold a text together
steps.sub: Read this before the texts. You will use it immediately.
steps.html:
Good writing does not repeat a noun phrase every time it is needed. It refers back to it with a small word, and the reader is expected to know which one is meant.

it refers to a specific thing already named. this and that can refer to a thing, but also to a whole idea in the previous sentence: Several studies have failed to find evidence for this.

one replaces a countable noun, so it can be counted and modified: the one nobody repeats, a stiff wire, and one that had been reported.

such means 'of that kind': Such occurrences are coincidence.

do so replaces a whole verb phrase in formal writing: The tilt would wander, and it would do so by a great deal. Compare in doing so, they started the myth.

When you meet one of these, stop and ask what exactly does this stand for? — and answer with the actual words from earlier in the text.

steps.title: Text A · What the counting showed
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Rotton & Kelly, Psychological Bulletin 97(2), 1985.

Ask ten people whether a full moon changes the way we behave, and most of them will say that it does. This is one of the most widespread beliefs in the world, and it survives in the absence of any supporting evidence at all. Nurses repeat it; so do police officers, and some of them will tell you that they can feel the difference on a busy night. That feeling is genuine. The pattern behind it is not.

The checking has been done, and it was done thoroughly. In 1985 two researchers collected thirty-seven published and unpublished studies of the supposed effect and combined them statistically, looking at hospital admissions, crisis calls, homicides and other criminal offences. A few individual results reached statistical significance; almost any large collection of studies will retain one or two of those. But when the whole set was measured together, the phase of the moon accounted for no more than one per cent of the variation in the behaviour usually described as lunacy. The authors advised that further work on the question was unnecessary. Forty years later, the belief is exactly where it was.

The reason it survives is not complicated. We notice the nights that fit the story and forget the ones that do not. A ward that is unusually lively during a full moon confirms the belief; a quiet one does nothing to it, because nobody retains a quiet Tuesday. Neither praise for the careful studies nor criticism of the sloppy ones has changed a single mind, and it is easy to see why: the belief was never built out of counted evidence in the first place, so counted evidence cannot take it apart.

steps.title: Text B · The same shape, in other stories
steps.html:
Written for this course.

Something similar happens with the physical explanation people offer. The moon moves the tides, they say, and we are mostly water, so it must move us as well. This sounds reasonable and is not. Tides are produced by the difference in pull across an entire ocean; on a body the size of a person that difference is smaller than the weight of a drop of sweat. The argument feels scientific because it uses the right vocabulary. That is a different thing from being correct.

Other beliefs of this kind are stranger. Millions of people are convinced that the 1969 landings were faked, and those who think so usually begin with the same detail: the flag appears to move, and there is no wind up there to make it do so. The explanation is accidental rather than deliberate. The pole was being twisted as it was pushed into the ground, and in the presence of no air to slow the motion, the movement simply continued for longer than it would here. A horizontal rod held the fabric out; that is why the flag looks as though it is flying.

What all of these have in common is an odd arithmetic. One unexplained detail counts as proof; a mountain of ordinary evidence counts as nothing. For centuries the moon was associated with madness and with evil, and now it is associated with conspiracy instead. The story changes; the shape of the reasoning does not. A cheerful belief and a depressing one turn out to be equally difficult to remove, which suggests that what people are defending is not the claim itself but the pleasure of having noticed something everybody else has missed.

steps.title: Choosing the right one
steps.html:
You have used them for reading. Now use them to stop repeating yourself.

it / they — a thing already named, with no emphasis. The moon affects the tides, but it does so only slightly.

this / these — something near, or the idea just stated, when you are about to say more about it. Several studies failed to find evidence for this.

that / those — something further away, or an idea you are stepping back from. That sounds implausible. A useful rule: this pulls the reader in, that holds the idea at arm's length.

one / ones — a countable noun, and you can put words in front of it: the one nobody repeats, a stiff wire, and one that had been reported. Never use one for an uncountable noun: I need advice — have you got one?

such — 'of the kind just described'. Such occurrences are coincidence.

do so / do that / do it — a whole verb phrase. Do so is the formal choice and is common in writing; do it is neutral.

steps.title: Removing a repetition
steps.html:
1. The draft: The moon affects the tides. The moon affects the tides only slightly.
  2. The second sentence repeats a noun and a verb phrase. Replace the noun with it: It affects the tides only slightly.
  3. Now the verb phrase repeats too. Replace it with do so: The moon affects the tides, but it does so only slightly.
  4. Check the reader can find the referent. It = the moon; does so = affects the tides. Both are in the sentence before.
  5. One more: if you wanted to step back from the whole idea, you would write That is worth remembering. — that, not it, because it refers to an idea rather than a thing.

steps.modelHtml:
Three things people believe about learning a language

There is almost no evidence for any of them, and that has never stopped anybody repeating them.

The first is that children learn faster than adults. Studies comparing the two under the same conditions find the opposite, and their absence from the popular account is itself revealing.

The second is that you must live in the country. This helps, obviously, but plenty of people move abroad and learn nothing; in doing so they prove that exposure alone does very little.

The third is that some people simply have no ear for languages. Such claims are almost always made by people who stopped after six weeks.

The one nobody repeats is the true one: that the strongest predictor is how many hours you have put in. That is dull, and it is worth remembering the next time somebody tells you they are just not a languages person.
